extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical literature and political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly commentary and critical notes on Books III–IV of Plato's Republic, extracting ethical, educational, stylistic and political standards embedded in the text. Focuses on the qualities required of guardians, judges, physicians, art, music, education and the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians must abstain from strong drink
rubrics_metrics.description: The guardians must abstain from strong drink, for they should be the last persons to lose their wits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a basic moral and practical requirement for those charged with the care of the State and its citizens; tied to the need for clear-headedness in rulers and protectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastic suited to guardians should be simple and wakeful
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary gymnastic is a sleepy sort of thing ... our warrior athletes must be wide-awake dogs, and must also be inured to all changes of food and climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Athletic training for guardians should be simpler and more robust than ordinary palaestra exercises, akin to their simple music—designed to keep them alert and resilient rather than merely ornamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dietary simplicity for guardians (Homeric rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: For their diet a rule may be found in Homer, who feeds his heroes on roast meat only, and gives them no fish ... nor boiled meats ... and, if I am not mistaken, he nowhere mentions sweet sauces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple, plain diet is prescribed to harden guardians and avoid luxuries that create softness; exotic or elaborate cookery (Sicilian cookery, Attic confections) must be forbidden as corrosive of virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid luxury and voluptuousness among guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Sicilian cookery and Attic confections and Corinthian courtezans ... must be forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luxury leads to gluttony and intemperance, which corrupt public life by creating unnecessary demand for lawyers and physicians and undermining civic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gluttony and intemperance — public cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Where gluttony and intemperance prevail the town quickly fills with doctors and pleaders; and law and medicine give themselves airs as soon as the freemen of a State take an interest in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public health and legal systems reflect private habits; excessive care of health and indulgence produces social ills and dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicians should not 'nurse' disease; prefer 'kill or cure' approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Asclepius would not practise this art, because he knew that the citizens of a well-ordered State have no leisure to be ill, and therefore he adopted the 'kill or cure' method ... They must be at their business, and have no time for coddling: if they recover, well; if they don't, there is an end of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical practice that manufactures chronic invalidism is condemned; medicine should serve the public interest by treating honest diseases and not prolonging weakness for profit or idleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge should be of a certain age and uncorrupted by crime
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge should be of a certain age; his youth should have been innocent, and he should have acquired insight into evil not by the practice of it, but by the observation of it in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because judges 'control mind by mind', their minds must not be corrupted by crime. Experience of vice should come through observation and discernment, not personal practice; youth is liable to be deceived by evildoers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance music and gymnastic to give harmony to the soul and health
rubrics_metrics.description: Good music which will give harmony to the soul, and good gymnastic which will give health to the body ... The two together supply our guardians with their twofold nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music tames and tempers the soul; gymnastic arouses and sustains it. Both arts concern the soul and must be combined in harmonious concord to produce ideal guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extremes: too much music or gymnastic corrupts character
rubrics_metrics.description: The passionate disposition when it has too much gymnastic is hardened and brutalized, the gentle or philosophic temper which has too much music becomes enervated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess of either art unbalances character: too little spirit is exhausted, too much leads to irritability; the ideal is a harmonious mixture that preserves reason and courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of rulers by life-long trials and tests
rubrics_metrics.description: These must be men who have been tried by many tests, like gold in the refiner's fire, and have been passed first through danger, then through pleasure, and at every age have come out of such trials victorious and without stain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulers are to be continuously observed and tested at every epoch of life to ensure constancy of principle under temptation, pleasure, pain and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a 'magnificent lie' (noble falsehood) to secure civic unity
rubrics_metrics.description: We will inform them that their youth was a dream ... and that they must protect and cherish her whose children they are, and regard each other as brothers and sisters ... others he made of silver ... but as they are all sprung from a common stock ... the son of the rich must descend, and the child of the artisan rise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A crafted myth told in hierarchical sequence (rulers, soldiers, people) can be employed as pedagogical fiction to instill brotherhood, social cohesion, and acceptance of role-transposition when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians must have no private property or wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: They should have no property; their pay should only meet their expenses; and they should have common meals ... They only of the citizens may not touch it, or be under the same roof with it, or drink from it, it is the accursed thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elimination of private property and wealth for guardians prevents the rise of householders, tradesmen and ultimately tyrants; material detachment is prescribed to secure impartial governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to Homer as authority used rhetorically
rubrics_metrics.description: The constant appeal to the authority of Homer, whom ... Plato summons as a witness about ethics and psychology, as well as about diet and medicine; attempting to distinguish the better lesson from the worse, sometimes altering the text from design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing an authoritative source can be a rhetorical vehicle for higher truth; Plato's use of Homer is sometimes figurative or a deliberate adaptation rather than strict exegesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style must conform to subject and metre to style
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The style is to conform to the subject and the metre to the style.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing should balance thought and expression: clarity, beauty, ease and proportion between style and subject are required; avoid obscurities where thought outstrips linguistic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: True art is simple, ideal, and moral
rubrics_metrics.description: True art is not fanciful and imitative, but simple and ideal,—the expression of the highest moral energy, whether in action or repose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should form natural good taste in youth, communicating truth and beauty across media; art functions as an aspect of reason in preliminary education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and music belong to education and shape character
rubrics_metrics.description: To live among works of plastic art which are of this noble and simple character, or to listen to such strains, is the best of influences,—the true Greek atmosphere, in which youth should be brought up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure to exemplary art and music in youth cultivates taste and moral feeling; art is an instrument of habituation in civic education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition of ranks: merit may break caste
rubrics_metrics.description: He also indicates that the system of caste ... should be set aside from time to time in favour of merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While acknowledging pre-existing distinctions, the state should allow occasional social mobility based on personal qualities—'the son of the rich must descend, and the child of the artisan rise.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and number have sacred, formative power
rubrics_metrics.description: There seems to mingle in Plato a sort of Pythagorean reverence for numbers and numerical proportion ... Intervals of sound and number are to him sacred things which have a law of their own, not dependent on the variations of sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato attributes to musical intervals and numerical proportion a formative influence on character and a metaphysical link with the world of ideas; the simple characteristic melody strongly affects the impressible mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind should control the body; seek harmony of reason and passion
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two principles in man, reason and passion ... The body becomes the good friend or ally, or servant or instrument of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical education aims to reconcile intellect and appetites so the mind governs bodily impulses; self-government and responsibility for health and conduct follow from this harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education must be primary; guardians should oversee education
rubrics_metrics.description: The care of the governors should be directed to preserve music and gymnastic ... When the wheel has once been set in motion, the speed is always increasing ... The guardians take care of education, and education will take care of all other things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education is the central institution that shapes character and institutions; good education prevents the need for minute legislation and sustains social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer middle economic condition for artisans and citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: A middle condition is best for artisans; they should have money enough to buy tools, and not enough to be independent of business. And will not the same condition be best for our citizens? If they are poor, they will be mean; if rich, luxurious and lazy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderate wealth ensures productivity and contentment; extremes of poverty or wealth corrupt social roles and civic stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the size of the State by the necessity of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: To the size of the state there is no limit but the necessity of unity; it must be neither too large nor too small to be one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political organisation must preserve unity; the appropriate scale of the polity is determined by its capacity to remain a single cohesive whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid minute enactments; culture and education govern manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute enactments are superfluous in good states, and are useless in bad ones ... Nor will any regulations be needed for the lesser matters of life—rules of deportment or fashions of dress. Like invites like for good or for evil. Education will correct deficiencies and supply the power of self-government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws should not attempt to micromanage private conduct; instead cultivate shared norms through education and cultural formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: First duty, then happiness — duty precedes utilitarian calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: First duty, then happiness, is the natural order of our moral ideas ... The greatest happiness of the individual may be the reverse of the greatest happiness ... The word 'happiness' has several ambiguities ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical and political aims prioritise right and duty; utilitarian considerations are secondary and serve as a corrective but not the foundation of morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice stylistic devices: affected ignorance, tentativeness, toggling reality/imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Lesser matters of style may be remarked. (1) The affected ignorance of music ... (2) The tentative manner in which ... he proceeds with the construction of the State. (3) The description of the State sometimes as a reality, and then again as a work of imagination only; ... (5) The companion pictures of the lover of litigation and the valetudinarian ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are observable rhetorical and compositional techniques by which Plato sustains interest, frames argument, and prepares for later developments (e.g., the expulsion of poets).
